column1: What is a package, in one sentence?
column2: Code somebody else wrote, downloaded as a file whose label carries a name and a version number.

column1: Which part of a package label changes constantly?
column2: The version number. The name almost never changes.

column1: Where do Python packages come from by default?
column2: PyPI, one enormous public index that anybody can publish to.

column1: What is a dependency?
column2: Code that other code needs in order to run at all.

column1: You run pip install rich and four packages arrive. What are the other three called?
column2: Dependencies — packages rich cannot run without, fetched automatically.

column1: In pip's output, what does the text beside a Collecting line mean?
column2: The constraint that dragged that package in, for example pygments<3.0.0,>=2.13.0.

column1: In pip install rich, which package asked for mdurl?
column2: markdown-it-py, not rich. That is a dependency two levels deep.

column1: Why does pip install packages in the order pygments, mdurl, markdown-it-py, rich?
column2: Dependency order — the deepest first, and the thing you asked for last.

column1: How many shelves does a machine have, without virtual environments?
column2: One, shared by every project on the machine.

column1: How many versions of a package can occupy one slot on that shared shelf?
column2: Exactly one.

column1: What happens when a second project needs a different version of a package already installed?
column2: The new install evicts the old one. The last install wins.

column1: Which pip lines show the eviction happening?
column2: Attempting uninstall, Found existing installation, Uninstalling, Successfully uninstalled.

column1: pip printed ERROR and then Successfully installed in the same run. What does that mean?
column2: pip broke a dependency of another package and completed the install anyway.

column1: After pip breaks a dependency, what happens when you run the affected code?
column2: Usually nothing. It keeps working until some other code path finally trips over the missing piece.

column1: Why does a broken environment cost so much time to diagnose?
column2: The break and the symptom are days apart, and the command that caused it reported success.

column1: Which command reports an inconsistent environment?
column2: pip check.

column1: What does ModuleNotFoundError usually mean, if you know you installed the package?
column2: The package is installed on a different environment from the one currently running.

column1: What are the two ways a Python project breaks?
column2: Loudly, with ModuleNotFoundError from the wrong environment; and silently, when one install overwrites a version another project needed.

column1: Which of those two failures is more expensive, and why?
column2: The silent one, because nothing announces it and there is no error to trace back.

column1: What is a virtual environment, in plain terms?
column2: A folder of packages that belongs to exactly one project.

column1: How does a virtual environment fix the version collision?
column2: Each project gets its own shelf, so two versions of the same package can exist at once.

column1: Why do so few beginners actually use virtual environments?
column2: The ritual — make it, activate it, remember which one you are in, deactivate it — and forgetting any step puts you back on the shared shelf.

column1: What does uv change about that ritual?
column2: uv creates, uses and forgets the environment for you, so there is nothing to remember.

column1: Compare a package and a dependency.
column2: A package is any installable unit. A dependency is a package required by another package rather than requested by you.
